newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Greek Cypriots start goodwill visit to N.Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: Greek Cypriots start goodwill visit to N.Cyprus.

text.p: More than 600 Greek Cypriots began a rare pilgrimage to a monastery in the Turkish-held part of Cyprus on Friday, a first since Turkey invaded the eastern Mediterranean island in 1974.

A bus convoy taking 650 Greek Cypriots with United Nations escorts set off at 8:15 a.m. (0515 GMT) from the U.N.-controlled Ledra Palace checkpoint, the only authorised crossing point between the north and south of the divided island.
Their destination was Apostolos Andreas, a monastery 125 km (80 miles) on the tip of the northeastern Karpasia peninsula.

Youngsters who have never been to the north of the ceasefire line slicing through Cyprus and pensioners travelled more than 100 km (60 miles) overnight to be at the checkpoint as dawn broke over Cyprus's capital Nicosia. Enthusiasm was tinged with sadness.
"I feel very touched. I haven't seen Apostolos Andreas for more than 23 years," said Charalambos Manolis, 37, a shipping surveyor who lives in the southern port town of Limassol.
The pilgrimage is one of a set of goodwill humanitarian gestures between the two sides to improve relations between Cyprus's estranged Greeks and Turks.
Instead of packing food and drinks, many brought with them two metre-long candles, olive oil and icons.
"It is for the family," said Manolis, gesturing to three large candles he was holding. "We light them in the church for a blessing from the saint."

As the Greek Cypriots waited for their buses on the edge of the Turkish held areas, they appeared oblivious to the large blue sign nearby saying "Welcome to the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus" , a breakaway state created in 1983 but recognised only by Turkey.
Turkey invaded the north of Cyprus in 1974 in response to a brief Greek Cypriot coup engineered by the military ruling Greece. Since then very few Greek Cypriots have been able to visit the north.
"I feel great joy, like an icon is in me, bless the Lord," enthused housewife Maria Valianti, 62, as she waited for a bus.
Valianti carried two large candlesticks with her. "I made this one 23 years ago," she said, touching the candle wrapped in newspaper. I have been waiting for this moment for years."
The monastery, built in 1867, is said to have been built on the spot where Apostole Andrew, one of Jesus's first disciples, ran aground during a missionary journey.
Before 1974 Greek Cypriots would hold an annual three-day vigil there on August 15, the day of the Assumption of the Virgin. It is one of the most important holidays in the Greek Orthodox calendar.
